World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Fourth man charged over alleged kidnapping murder of Chris Baghsarian
World.content:
A fourth man has been charged in relation to the alleged kidnapping and murder of a Sydney grandfather.

Chris Baghsarian was taken from his North Ryde home in a case of mistaken identity just after 5am on February 13.

The 85-year-old's abduction triggered an 11-day search, with his remains later found near a golf course in Pitt Town in the city's north-west.

Chris Baghsarian's remains were found in north-west Sydney following an 11-day search. (ABC News)

It is understood his captors' intended target was a relative of Sydney businessman Dimitri Stepanyan, who also lived nearby.

On Tuesday morning, detectives arrested a fourth man — aged 19 — at Mount Druitt Police Station.

He was charged with murder and take or detain in company with intent to ransom occasioning actual bodily harm.

Three other men remain before the courts.

He was refused bail and is due to appear in Mount Druitt Local Court today.

World.title: Junior clubs and brain experts welcome NRL training changes
World.content:
Junior rugby league clubs and neuroscientists have welcomed changes by the National Rugby League (NRL) to address growing concerns around injuries but say more should be done to protect children.

The ABC revealed on Tuesday the NRL has introduced caps on contact in training in a bid to reduce injuries, including concussions.

Under the new rules, during the current men's season clubs are restricted to engaging in no more than 100 minutes of contact training on a seven-day turnaround.

The new guidelines bring the NRL more in line with other high-contact sports. (ABC News)

When the 2027 preseason starts after Christmas, they will be restricted to no more than 200 minutes of contact training per week.

In the NRLW, which begins in July, female players will be able to engage in no more than 85 minutes per week on a seven-day turnaround, and 115 minutes during their next preseason.

All of this training is inclusive of wrestling.

'Not a badge of honour'

Long-term exposure to head trauma, common in football codes in Australia, has been linked to the progressive brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

President of Townsville-based junior rugby league club JCU Saints and former player Sean Evans said the more knowledge gained about the effects of ongoing concussion, the better.

He said he was a "big fan" of the changes.

Sean Evans has seen the impacts of CTE on former players and welcomes the changes. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"From an ex-player, I've seen a lot of the effects of what CTE has on people," he said.

"The more protection we can offer the kids, especially starting so young, the better. It'll trickle up throughout their whole career."

Sean Evans says the JCU Saints are always looking for ways to reduce the physical stress on young players. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Swinburne Adjunct Professor and research manager at the Australian Sports Brain Bank Alan Pearce said making changes to address how many head knocks younger players had would help improve their longevity post-career.

"Unfortunately, unless we do something about it now, we're just going to see young players ... suffering from early onset dementias and movement disorders and cognitive impairments and mental health issues," he said.

" So, this is something that we can't keep kicking the can down the road. "

Dr Alan Pearce says the new guidelines don't go far enough and society isn't moving fast enough to address the problem. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Mr Evans said his club was always looking for ways to reduce the physical stress on young players.

He said it could be "tricky" to find a balance between preparing kids for the realities of the sport and protecting their health.

"Trying to implement [full contact] in increments is, I think, the best way to do it," he said.

"Start them small, just do a couple of little sort of contact sessions without going to the ground and then slowly pick it up from there."

Inside a brain with suspected CTE The effect of head knocks over Gordi Kirkbank-Ellis's decades-long sporting career isn't immediately obvious. That is, until you see what's happening to his brain.

'Good start' but not far enough

The youngest brain with diagnosed CTE in the Australian Brain Bank is 20 years old, Dr Pearce said, while the youngest in the United States is 17.

"It's not a badge of honour to have a concussion, especially as a kid," Dr Pearce said.

"We have to get parents to understand that this is not a head knock, this is actually a brain injury.

"We don't tolerate other types of injuries, for shoulders or hamstrings, and we've got to have the same attitude — if not stricter — for children's brains.

"That's why it's so important that we put these limits in."

The ABC revealed on Tuesday the NRL has introduced caps on contact in training in a bid to reduce injuries, including concussions. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Dr Pearce said the changes were a "good start" but more had to be done.

"I certainly think that we can go further, as we get more data on the effectiveness of the current policy," he said.

"I think we need to start to think about aligning with other sports like rugby union, which has 15 minutes full contact per week."

Russell says parents are always worrying about head knocks. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

JCU Saints referee and parent Russell said the potential for head knocks was in the "back of every parent's mind".

"I think that we need to put a huge onus on empowering and protecting our referees to enforce the Safe Play Code, which is only relevant to under-16s," he said.

"Within most regional rugby league communities, you'll have some old-and-bolds that are always like, 'it was harder in my day, it was tougher in my day'.

"They stand in the way of progress at times, which can be a little bit disappointing."

World.title: Carpooling an 'effective solution' to fuel prices, so why aren't more doing it?
World.content:
Frustrated by the current petrol prices, primary school teacher Blanche Sayers is about to start carpooling with a colleague.

They both live in the Hobart suburb of Mount Nelson and have given each other lifts before, but never considered regular carpooling until the current fuel crisis.

"It just seemed like a sensible solution to save a little bit of money," Ms Sayers said.

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

Carpooling is one of the "travel alternatives" being promoted by the Australian government as part of the national fuel security plan.

In a list of fuel-saving tips, the Department of Infrastructure suggested "getting to a destination with a few friends nearby could be a great way to do your bit".

But while some people, like Ms Sayers, have managed to embrace shared commutes quite easily — others have found it more difficult.

The federal Department of Infrastructure has suggested carpooling as a way for people to save money on petrol. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Increase of just 1 per cent in Sydney carpooling lane

Multiple people contacted for this story said they were unable to find anyone to carpool with, despite reaching out to their community.

There is also very limited data available to track whether more people are adopting the behaviour.

Fuel crisis mean some young Australians cannot get to work Young people are taking extraordinary steps to deal with the fuel crisis, including cutting back on work because the cost of fuel to get there more than they will be paid.

Transit lanes, typically signposted as T2 or T3, are designated lanes restricted to vehicles carrying multiple passengers, designed to promote carpooling.

New South Wales is the only state or territory that tracks the number of vehicles using the lanes, which are also available to electric vehicles and public transport.

According to Transport for NSW, about 206,000 vehicles used the T3 lane on Spit Road, heading towards the Sydney CBD, on weekday mornings in February.

That figure rose to about 209,000 in March — an increase of just 1 per cent — despite the start of the current Middle East conflict causing higher fuel prices.

There is limited information available to measure the uptake of carpooling in Australia. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

Australians struggle to embrace carpooling, expert says

The perceived lack of uptake is unsurprising for Hussein Dia, who is a Professor of Transport, Technology and Sustainability at Swinburne University.

He said carpooling in Australia had "never picked up" despite concerted efforts from the sustainability sector over the past four decades.

"In theory, it is very effective because people are sharing a vehicle between two or three people, which can reduce the fuel use and cost per person," Professor Dia said.

" People want to do it and they're keen to do it, but the underlying systems and support systems are not there. "

Hussein Dia says carpooling has "never picked up" in Australia, despite efforts from the sustainability sector. (Supplied: Hussein Dia)

The census in 2021, conducted during the COVID pandemic, found that of the roughly 6.8 million responders who travelled to work in a car, only 6 per cent were passengers.

Professor Dia said the key hurdle for most Australians was finding someone whose schedule aligned for the commute both to and from work.

"People have different work schedules and nowadays we even have hybrid days, so people's schedules in many cases are not aligned," he said.

Awareness campaign 'unlikely' to drive widespread uptake

If the federal government were serious about increasing carpooling rates, Professor Dia said the focus would need to shift to establishing enabling conditions.

Taxi drivers' fuel price concerns Country taxi drivers say the fuel crisis could prove to be the death knell for the industry.

He said this could include workplace-based coordination, digital matching platforms, and targeted incentives that make shared travel more attractive.

"Awareness campaigns on their own are unlikely to drive widespread uptake [of carpooling]," Professor Dia said.

"One of the most practical approaches is workplace coordination … where employers actively help staff to organise shared travel, rather than leaving it to individuals.

Discounts on toll roads and free parking at workplaces were other incentives that he suggested could help drive more people to share their commute.

He said digital platforms that match together commuters looking to head in the same direction were a growing trend that could prove effective in major cities.

Francois Chemillier started developing his app after seeing the number of single-occupant cars stuck in traffic in Sydney's northern beaches. (Supplied: Francois Chemillier)

Carpooling should be promoted beyond fuel crisis, app developer says

Francois Chemillier, who lives in Sydney's Northern Beaches, is part of this wave — having just launched his own carpooling app.

He was inspired to pull the platform together two years ago, due to the number of single-occupant vehicles stuck in traffic each day near his home.

"[Carpooling] is really the most effective solution right now for Australians to adopt, to limit the use of fuel," Mr Chemillier said.

"But without the proper technology, you won't easily find someone who goes where you want to go, the same day at the same time."

As well as saving money, Blanche Sayers says she's looking forward to having company during her commute. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

Mr Chemillier was hopeful that digital platforms like his could be key in making carpooling more accessible and helping to drive behavioural change.

He said the government should continue to promote the practice beyond the current fuel crisis, due to its environmental and social benefits.

Beyond simply saving money, Ms Sayers said she felt her plans to start carpooling with her colleague would also provide a positive social outlet.

"It will be nice just travelling with a colleague and having somebody to talk to in the morning and afternoon," she said.

World.title: Closure of specialist centres for children with autism puts spotlight on NDIS funding
World.content:
Five-year-old Dimitri Moore has suffered a "massive deterioration in his behaviour" since the abrupt closure of Australia's AEIOU centres for children with autism.

Queensland-based Dimitri attended an AEIOU centre four days a week from January last year until last month, when the not-for-profit AEIOU Foundation ceased all its services.

Dimitri Moore received behavioural therapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy, as well as day care, at an AEIOU centre. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Australia's 11 AEIOU centres in Queensland, Adelaide, and Canberra were a one-stop shop for children with autism, providing long daycare and therapies under the one roof. For many parents, the centres allowed them to continue working.

Their closure has put a spotlight on the adequacy of National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) funding for children with "severe, profound, lifelong" autism.

Federal Health Minister Mark Butler is expected to outline further changes to address ballooning costs to the $50 billion scheme later today.

Before the AEIOU shutdown, Dimitri's single dad Eric Moore said his son was slowly learning how to communicate after 14 months of intensive therapy at the Bald Hills centre, in Brisbane's north.

Eric Moore says Dimitri made slow, but consistent, progress during his 14 months at an AEIOU centre. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

While his little boy speaks only in a few words, Mr Moore said Dimitri was able to follow simple instructions and was slowly developing life skills, such as learning to use a toilet, because of the evidence-based AEIOU program.

"His understanding has vastly improved," the 34-year-old teacher said.

"We started learning some basic ways to communicate back and forth. He started being more expressive of his needs. That's been a benefit for his general wellbeing."

But after more than a year of slow but consistent progress, Mr Moore said Dimitri had regressed since the sudden shuttering of the AEIOU centres, leaving hundreds of children and their families in limbo.

"We've seen a massive deterioration in his behaviour," Mr Moore said.

" His routines and everything need to be completely rebuilt. We have to find him new therapists. "

But he describes his and Dimitri's situation as more fortunate than most, citing cases of parents having to negotiate time off work or quit their jobs entirely to take care of their children since the AEIOU shutdown.

"It just up-ends a lot of people's lives," Mr Moore said.

Eric Moore says Dimitri’s behaviour has deteriorated since the closure of his AEIOU centre. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

He's been able to enrol Dimitri in Pine Rivers Special School, north of Brisbane, but is gutted by the loss of AEIOU in his son's life.

"When they have a consistent team that all works together … a lot of these children have had, over the years that AEIOU operated … awesome outcomes," Mr Moore said.

"There are kids who go to the school that I teach at now who are doing apprenticeships, who are becoming members of the workforce, who are doing really well, who went to AEIOU back in the early days."

NDIS cuts blamed

The AEIOU Foundation went into liquidation after more than two decades of providing specialised early intervention services for thousands of children with autism.

Children with autism forced out of specialised program due to NDIS funding cuts A service for children with autism say they have been overwhelmed by reports from parents saying their NDIS payments have been being slashed by up to 60 per cent when their plans are reviewed.

AEIOU parents and staff have blamed the collapse on cuts to the NDIS packages of many of the children attending the centres.

Cancer specialist James Morton, who founded the AEIOU Foundation in 2005 after his own son's autism diagnosis, hit out at management of the NDIS for the foundation's demise.

Dr Morton said that in 2024, the packages of many children attending AEIOU centres had been cut dramatically.

He said NDIS delegates also started telling parents wanting to access an AEIOU centre for their children that the "AEIOU is not funded by the NDIS, their child should go to mainstream and learn from other children".

"They made statements like: "AEIOU does not align with the NDIS,'" Dr Morton said. "Our numbers dropped and the funding that we had for the children plummeted.

"The problem is that the children and their needs are so complex that the standard childcare system can't cope with them.

"It's not a blame on the childcare system. It's a reflection on the level of developmental delay that these children have."

Dr Morton said putting a child who was non-verbal, not toilet trained and with high levels of social anxiety into mainstream childcare was "unreasonable" and "diabolical policy".

Children frequently started at the AEIOU with challenging behaviours, including head banging and biting, he said.

"Eighty per cent of families enrolled their children in mainstream childcare prior to attending AEIOU and had to leave due to their child being unable to participate, not making any gains, or due to challenging behaviours," Dr Morton said.

Australia's 11 AEIOU centres in Queensland, Adelaide, and Canberra provided long daycare and therapies under the one roof. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

After the AEIOU centres' closure, he said one child had been rejected by 50 childcare centres, and another by 18.

Dr Morton said the AEIOU Foundation's closure would send the care of children with "severe and profound" autism "back to the Dark Ages" and would result in bigger costs for the NDIS moving forward.

"It's just the most shattering thing," he said.

"It's hard for me as a doctor, where every decision we make is evidence based, to understand what the NDIS has done in this space and what they call evidence, which is no evidence at all.

"The whole of government cost of 40 children with profound autism coming to AEIOU, compared to the same 40 children going to their local childcare centres, and accessing community-based therapy, is the same. But the developmental outcomes are very different."

In 2021 the AEIOU Foundation opened a centre in Canberra. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Dr Morton said about half of the 3,300 children who had attended an AEIOU centre since 2005 ended up being able to attend a mainstream school.

"About 80 per cent of children leave AEIOU with the ability to communicate, 70 per cent leave toilet trained," Dr Morton said.

Griffith University autism researcher Jessica Paynter, who previously worked for the AEIOU Foundation, said children attending the centres were assessed when they entered the program, at 12 months, and when they left.

"The research tended to show positive outcomes for both children and their families," the clinical psychologist said.

Griffith University autism researcher Jessica Paynter. (Supplied)

Dr Paynter described the loss of the AEIOU centres as "unacceptable".

"We can't have families having supports that have wrapped around them just pulled out from under them," she said.

"AEIOU's been around for 20 years. That's a lot of experience and skills that have been developed over time that have now been lost."

Dr Paynter said services should be seen as an investment, rather than a cost.

"I'm really concerned by the rhetoric that is emerging quite strongly at the moment about cost and the need to cut," she said.

"These are human lives that we're investing in.

"By cutting funds from one place, such as the NDIS, we're only going to increase costs in other places, such as mental health, emergency wards or education settings."

Canberra-based Martin Laverty, who was on the first National Disability Insurance Agency board and is now the chief executive of Aruma disability services, said not-for-profit NDIS providers were facing "viability pressures" after a "seven-year freeze in therapy pricing".

Dr Martin Laverty, who was on the first National Disability Insurance Agency board and is now chief executive of Aruma disability services. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Dr Laverty said the freeze had driven organisations, such as the AEIOU Foundation, out of business and predicted more would follow.

"Very sadly, the AEIOU Foundation won't be the last to exit the NDIS because of the seven-year freeze," he said.

"For those children, young people and families that were supported by the AEIOU Foundation and other therapy providers who have exited, those families have been left with uncertain futures, not clear about where they might find their services elsewhere."

Parents shocked by sudden closure of specialist service for kids with autism Parents left shocked by abrupt closure of Brisbane specialist service for children with autism.

Children under nine years old with mild to moderate autism will transition off the NDIS and onto a program dubbed Thriving Kids from October.

But those deemed to have "significant permanent disability", such as Dimitri, who was diagnosed as a two-and-a-half-year-old with level 3 autism — requiring the highest support needs — will remain on NDIS funding.

Mr Moore said Dimitri attended three mainstream daycare centres before going to AEIOU.

He was asked to leave the first two and was having regular meltdowns at the third.

Dimitri Moore, 5, was able to attend an AEIOU centre for four days a week. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

After initially being rejected for NDIS funding for Dimitri to attend an AEIOU centre, Mr Moore was successful in a much "more thorough" reapplication, showing "AEIOU was the most cost-effective option".

"I mathed out that — if he can't attend daycare I have to quit work," the young dad said.

"For a lot of families, they don't have the time, the energy, the resources or the capacity to navigate such a complex system.

"Fo so many others, it's a matter of getting what they're given. It is grossly unfair because it is the children ultimately who suffer."

At AEIOU, Dimitri received behavioural therapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy as well as day care, all at the one centre, four days a week.

Dimitri Moore is one of about 3,300 children who have attended an AEIOU centre since 2005. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Despite AEIOU's success with children over many years, federal NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister said the scheme funded individual supports "in line with a child's assessed needs and developmental goals, not entire programs of support designed by providers".

An NDIS spokesman said the agency administering the NDIS was "working closely with families and partners to assist children to transition to alternative services" since the AEIOU centre closures.

"Anyone needing help should contact their early childhood partner or the NDIS," the spokesman said.

Queensland Disability Services Minister Amanda Camm said the state's Education Department was offering support to assist families to find alternate care and education for AEIOU participants.

World.title: The growing problem stopping Melbourne residents using their microwave
World.content:
Marie Slako moved into her Northcote home two years ago, attracted to the property for its rooftop solar and partial conversion to electricity-powered heating and appliances.

"I'd like to get off fossil fuels," Ms Slako said. "And also gas is really expensive. The winter price, it hurts."

But shortly after moving in, problems started to occur.

First, Ms Slako noticed she could only use one hotplate at a time on her induction cooktop. Then she found the microwave would not heat food at dinnertime, but would burn everything at other times.

Earlier this month, she discovered her split system would not heat the house.

Marie Slako was mystified as to why her electrical appliances were not working as they should. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"The cold weekend we just had, I could not get the split system to work at all, which is pretty annoying," Ms Slako said.

"There's a sense of dread waiting for winter when I'm cold, and the split system's not heating reliably. I might have to look at what else I can do, like reinvigorating the old gas heating, which is going to cost a lot.

"I have noticed things are getting worse; it wasn't this bad last year."

Marie Slako is dreading winter with a house full of underperforming appliances. (ABC News)

After discovering the issues stemmed from the house's power supply, Ms Slako called network operator CitiPower and found the issue was something called undervoltage.

So many homes on Ms Slako's street had transitioned from gas to electricity that the infrastructure could not push through enough electricity to homes to run appliances reliably during peak times.

Induction cooktops were not working. EV chargers were disconnecting, leaving cars without battery. Heaters were struggling to push out hot air.

CitiPower manager of customer planning and power quality Tom Langstaff uses the analogy of being in a hot shower when someone in the house starts washing the dishes and turning on other taps.

The hot water system cannot push through enough heated water, and the shower runs cold. Similarly, if the electricity demand is too high in some areas, the voltage plummets and certain appliances stop working.

Tom Langstaff says Victoria's infrastructure is being put under strain by increased electricity demand. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

"[The power network] was sort of designed to handle customers' consumption for a given time when it was originally built," Mr Langstaff said.

"As we're seeing customers draw more and more power through that network, it comes under pressure.

"It's definitely a rapid growth in electrification that's occurring, and then that really challenges our networks."

Undervoltage issue grows as Victorians give up gas

CitiPower says undervoltage is a growing problem, exacerbated by more Victorians getting off gas.

The network operator, which distributes power to more than 300,000 customers in metropolitan Melbourne, says smart meter analysis shows the average energy consumption on cold days has jumped fourfold for customers who have removed gas connections and electrified their homes.

Complaints received by the operator include customers being unable to heat or cool their homes, EV chargers not working, and broken or malfunctioning appliances.

The undervoltage issue meant Marie Slako could only partially use her induction cooktop. (ABC News)

To address what it sees as a growing problem, CitiPower has lodged a submission with the Australian Energy Regulator (AER) seeking a greater revenue allowance for both proactive and reactive improvements to networks at risk of undervoltage problems.

Every five years, network providers such as CitiPower must lodge their spending applications with the AER for a review of the revenue they can collect from customers for network maintenance and upgrades.

CitiPower said its latest submission would not increase electricity bills.

"We see that electrification will grow, and with that, we expect that the issues the customers will face through that period will grow as well," Mr Langstaff said.

"Our plan is to be proactive, to get ahead of this and make sure that we're there for customers when they want safe and reliable power."

The AER has previously declined a similar proposal, arguing CitiPower had overstated the impacts of undervoltage.

Undervoltage not a reason to delay transition to electricity, experts say

Victoria Energy Policy Centre director Bruce Mountain said the issue of undervoltage came amid Victoria's energy transition, with households encouraged to move away from gas.

But he said undervoltage was not yet a major cause for concern.

"This is not yet a widespread problem," Professor Mountain said.

"I think it's a matter of understanding how the evolution of these demands, and battery, and solar, and the simultaneous use of all of these will occur, and we have yet to see how that's going to take place."

CitiPower is pushing for more investment into electrical infrastructure to match demand. (ABC News)

The director of the Centre for Smart Power and Energy Research, Saman A Gorji, said undervoltage should not be used as an argument against electrification.

"As more households add EV charging, electric heating, and other new electric loads, some older low-voltage networks can experience voltage drops when several loads are active simultaneously," Dr Gorji said.

"That does not mean electrification is the wrong direction. It means parts of the grid need to catch up.

"The answer is targeted local upgrades, better data, and smarter demand management — not a retreat from electrification."

World.title: In a split second, Keelie made the 'surreal' decision to reveal her abuse
World.content:
In mid-2019, Keelie McMahon was sitting with her mum at their family home when suddenly the topic changed.

"Have you heard [someone] has gone to the police and made a report about sexual abuse?" her mother asked.

Ms McMahon hadn't heard.

"She's claiming James Griffin abused her."

In that split second, Ms McMahon knew she had a decision to make.

James Geoffrey Griffin, a family friend, had worked as a registered nurse at Launceston General Hospital's Paediatric Centre and as a massage therapist for children's sporting teams.

He was an active and well-liked member of the community.

He had also groomed and sexually abused an unknown number of the children who were placed in his care.

One of them was Keelie McMahon.

"In that moment, I chose to tell my mum that I, too, had been abused," she tells the ABC now, seven years after that first disclosure.

"It was like the world stopped spinning.

"It was a very surreal feeling, I suppose.

" This secret that I'd kept for nearly 10 years at that point had just come out into the open, and it was something that I'd never considered actually talking about. "

In the months that followed Griffin would be charged and accused of historic sexual abuse of at least five young girls, some dating as far back as the 1980s.

That October he took his own life, ensuring he would never face court for his crimes.

Keelie McMahon says more awareness of sexual abuse may have made her speak up sooner. (Supplied)

"I think people underestimate the impact that something like sexual violence can have on a person's life, especially when it happens at a young age," Ms McMahon said.

"It completely rewrites the course of a child's life when they're sexually abused.

"It is getting more traction than it would have in the past, but it's still one of those things where people [think] we can't talk about this, we can't teach our children about this.

"I feel in a way people are desensitised to it. They're just like, 'Oh, it's part of life.'"

Estimated 2.8 million suffer sexual violence

A national discussion about sexual violence is long overdue, according to Nicole Lambert, chair of the National Association of Services Against Sexual Violence (NASASV).

An estimated 89,400 people aged 18 and over experienced sexual assault across Australia in 2024-2025, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

What is sexual violence? Sexual violence is an umbrella term referring to any sexual behaviours or acts committed against a person's will — including sexual assault, sexual harassment, threats, exploitation, child abuse and more.

In its last Personal Safety Survey in 2022, the ABS estimated 2.8 million people aged 18 and older had experienced sexual violence since the age of 15.

The 2023 Child Maltreatment Study estimated about 28.5 per cent of Australians had experienced sexual abuse before the age of 18.

At the other end of the spectrum, the aged care royal commission found there were approximately 50 sexual assaults recorded every week in residential aged care.

As the nation marks Sexual Assault Awareness Month, Ms Lambert says it remains one of the most pervasive and under-reported forms of violence in Australia today.

"At the moment, sexual assault services right across the country are just absolutely buckling under the weight of demand," she said.

"They've seen no significant increase in investment in the sexual violence response, prevention, healing and recovery services, or crisis response, in decades.

"When you look at investment in the sexual violence space compared to the family and domestic violence space, just the size of the underinvestment is really just astounding. It's huge.

" We know that means there are tens of thousands of victim-survivors that are going without support because the services just can't meet demand. "

The federal government announced a 72 per cent funding boost for frontline family, domestic and sexual violence workforces in March.

The $291.7 million announcement was to boost the "vital" work of creating new homes and offering legal support to women escaping violence.

"Frontline workers are … the people answering the call during a crisis, providing safety and security, and supporting women and children to rebuild their lives," Assistant Minister for the Prevention of Family Violence Ged Kearney said.

Ms Lambert noted sexual violence and family and domestic violence (FDV) were often conflated, rather than seen as separate problems.

Resource to help 'invisible' older women victim-survivors Experts say sexual violence against older women is "grossly underestimated" as victim-survivors face additional barriers to disclosing the abuse.

"Sexual violence can occur within family and domestic violence so it can be used as a tactic of FDV," she said.

"But obviously there's a huge amount of sexual violence that occurs outside of a family and domestic violence context.

"Because the two issues are often conflated, I think governments and policymakers often feel that they've covered off on sexual violence already.

"There's this assumption that 'We've already done that', when that's not actually the case.

"And often when we speak about sexual violence … we can see that people's attention has refocused back in on family violence. They're really only thinking about the sexual violence that occurs within that context."

Survivors 'deserve to tell the universe that what happened'

James Geoffrey Griffin had been the subject of multiple allegations of abuse.

Tasmania Police received information about potential child abuse perpetrated by Griffin in 2009, 2011, 2013 and 2015, according to an internal review.

Ms McMahon, now 29, still grapples with the amount of time it took for someone to take action against the nurse.

Keelie McMahon, pictured around the time of the sexual abuse by James Geoffrey Griffin. (Supplied)

She also wonders what difference it would have made if the abuse had been happening on the mainland.

"Tasmania sometimes feels like it's 20 years in the past when it comes to certain things like this," Ms McMahon says.

"We are very delayed in catching up with social norms down here, unfortunately.

"I feel like that may have had a big impact [on me] because when I think back to when I first made my report, I knew of no services that helped with sexual violence.

"I feel like if I had had the same education that my children have around body safety and body boundaries, I would have known from the start of the abuse that it was not OK.

"I know that, looking back, deep down I knew that something wasn't right.

"But because I hadn't heard about it or I hadn't had open conversations about it, I didn't think that I needed to say something to protect myself.

"Had I had that experience … I probably would have spoken up a lot sooner."

Keelie McMahon is now a social worker and advocate. (Supplied)

She is now a social worker and also acts as a lived experience advocate for Laurel House, a not-for-profit sexual assault support service operating across northern Tasmania.

"I think while it's important to acknowledge that there are victim-survivors that want to keep their trauma close to their chest, and how strong they are for making that decision … I use my voice to show people they don't have to feel ashamed of what happened to them," Ms McMahon says.

"They deserve to heal loudly, if that's what they want to do. They deserve to tell the universe that what happened to them wasn't fair.

"We're moving into an age where these things need to not be silenced. People need to feel like they're taken seriously when they speak about these things.

"The most important thing to me is making sure that people know the impact that abuse can have on other people, so that they actually take it seriously and become a voice as well to say that this needs to stop."

Becoming a victim-survivor after years as a support person

Ayla Williams has always been passionate about preventing sexual violence against women.

The 27-year-old from Tasmania had already been through having a close family member impacted by historical rape.

"They didn't report for many understandable reasons, but I experienced some impact of what happened to them in a very real and ongoing way. It's something I now recognise as vicarious trauma," she says.

"Witnessing and being part of their process was deeply eye-opening for one, but almost cathartic in terms of the dynamic of our relationship."

Ayla Williams endured a three-year battle in the judicial system after deciding to raise her voice. (Supplied)

But a few years later, things took a turn.

"I was raped in September 2020 by someone that myself and my immediate family were housing," Ms Williams says.

"He'd been through a divorce and wasn't having contact with his children … we'd housed him and were providing a support network ot try and help him get back on his feet.

"We had an established relationship and it was a friendship I had come to value."

She had already turned down some advances from her attacker before the incident occurred.

According to the ABS, only 6.1 per cent of women in Australia experienced sexual violence by a male stranger.

Twenty per cent — equivalent to 2 million women nationwide — had experienced sexual violence by a man already familiar to them.

The costly fight for justice

Her past experience led Ms Williams to report the rape soon after.

“There is an incomprehensible cost regardless of the path taken, but the cost of not reporting to me personally was too great," she says.

It was a decision that triggered a three-year process "fully entwined within the legal system".

"I found it was almost like a lottery … your experience with whatever service was really dependent on who was on the other end of the phone [or] on the other side of the receptionist desk," Ms Williams says.

"Some exchanges and interactions with people working in the legal system, in various departments, made me feel so reduced and minimised, and like an inconvenience.

"It was those things … that made me almost throw in the towel."

Loading...

The perpetrator ultimately pleaded guilty and was sentenced to four years behind bars in October 2023.

Like Ms McMahon, Ms Williams is now a lived experience advocate for Laurel House — a role she says she took on out of need to "create something" from her ordeal.

"I think we've made a lot of progress, I can definitely see and hear and feel that, particular in societal attitudes," Ms Williams says.

"But are we near the end? Far from it, in my opinion."

'Committed to evolving with it and through it'

Looking back on that split second decision to disclose her own abuse, Ms McMahon has a message for her 22-year-old self.

"There were a lot of times when I was like, 'This isn't worth it, I don't want to do this,'" she says.

"Being able to show her the change that has come from the disclosures that were made by myself and other people, being able to explain how many bad people have been stopped.

"I feel like that would be really important to keep past me going, knowing what was coming."

For Ms Williams, the version of herself that existed before experiencing sexual violence "is gone".

"I still grieve, I still mourn, and I think there'll be an element of me that will [stay] for the remainder of my life," she says.

"But I'm committed to evolving with it and through it."

To her younger self, she says: "You're going to learn very quickly that truth, law and justice can exist on completely different tracks".

"What you experienced was very real, but the system you're about to enter is going to need it to be measurable," she says.

"We all have a basic human right to seek legal recourse when a crime is committed against us, but when that train leaves the station, there's no getting off it.

"I purposely don't call it a justice system when I'm talking about my own personal experience — I prefer to call it a judicial system, because I think law and justice aren't always mutually exclusive.

"You've really just got to dig deep."

Loading...

Need for more funding, dedicated sexual violence framework

Last year the Australian Law Reform Commission (ALRC) published the results of its Justice Responses to Sexual Violence inquiry.

The report noted that nine out of 10 women did not report sexual violence to the police and that their experience with the justice system was "re-traumatising".

Fixing the problem would require "substantial action from almost every government system".

Access to resources, access to the justice system and access to key support was noted as a major issue in the total 64 recommendations made by the commission.

Ms Lambert knows a dedicated sexual violence prevention framework would make a difference to an already existing sector of more than 120 services nationwide.

Calls for anonymous sexual violence reporting RMIT University's criminologist Georgina Heydon says more than 90 per cent of sexual violence incidents in Victoria go unreported.

"The investment needs to go into expanding that sector … because without that, we don't have the resources to scale up to meet demand," she says.

"Currently there's a lot of people throughout the country that really don't have access to forensic and medical responses, not timely access anyway.

"It might require them to drive or fly for several hours to get to a location where [it is] available, which for a lot of people, after the unspeakable kind of trauma they've experienced, is not realistic.

"They just don't have the support, energy or resources to go ahead with that.

"They'd rather try their best to put it behind them and get on with things, which is only going to leave them without support and likely to compound future impacts."

World.title: 500,000 Australians wait for end to 'limbo' as Butler readies NDIS plan
World.content:
National Disability Insurance Scheme Minister Mark Butler must end the "limbo" half a million Australians have been living in when he announces changes to the nation's disability scheme, mental health advocates say.

The federal government is on a collision course with the states over the future of hundreds of thousands of Australians living with mental illness who are languishing outside the NDIS, as it moves to restrict access to psychosocial support through the scheme.

There are about 66,000 people on the NDIS with conditions such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, but the Productivity Commission has identified about 500,000 people who also have moderate to severe psychosocial illness but do not receive support through the NDIS or any other government-funded programs, with many state services collapsing after the NDIS was created.

In 2023 federal and state governments agreed to create services outside the NDIS to support that cohort, following the creation of a similar "foundational support" service for children with mild to moderate autism.

But little has changed since the agreement was made.

Mr Butler will address the National Press Club today, and is expected to detail changes to the NDIS that are designed to slow its growing expenses to 5 to 6 per cent a year — or more than $6 billion a year — by 2036.

The mandatory registration of providers, changes to pricing rules, limits to participant plans and tightening of Supported Independent Living are all reforms under consideration by the government.

Anxiety over restricted access

The psychosocial disability community fears it could be a target of savings measures and that people with mental illness could be diverted from the NDIS to state services yet to be created.

Ian Hickie from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Centre said he anticipated that the federal government would move to ring-fence those already on the NDIS for psychosocial support, diverting access to others in need.

"There's been real anxiety that mental health or the psychosocial disability might be the sacrificial lamb on the altar of NDIS reform," he said.

Ian Hickie says the community is anxious about the next round of reforms. (ABC News: Bryan Milliss)

A report by the Australian Psychosocial Alliance found that barriers for people with mental illness to access the NDIS were already increasing, with people with psychosocial conditions who applied to the NDIS receiving access half as often as all other cohorts, leaving more without support over time.

Psychosocial Alliance chair Debra Zanella said it was time for Mr Butler to clarify how people would be supported both in and out of the NDIS.

"I would be hoping that the minister honours the commitment to investment in 'foundational supports' outside the NDIS — the recognition that there are people with psychosocial disability who belong in the scheme, for which the scheme was designed for," she said.

"And [I hope] that there is some articulation, today, of clarity around those people who do have a psychosocial disability and don't need to be in the scheme, that we have a very clear pathway for that support across Australia outside the NDIS.

"It is 'and' — it is not 'either-or.'

"People with a psychosocial disability do belong in the scheme … they have a long-term, permanent, functional disability that impacts on their ability to live a good life, and they require a good life."

Deb Zanella says there must be pathways for psychosocial supports in and out of the NDIS. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Ms Zanella said she would be "highly surprised" if the government decided psychosocial conditions were not considered in need of NDIS support.

She noted costs for participants on the NDIS with psychosocial disability were growing within the incoming target band of 5 to 6 per cent, and there would be limited savings to be achieved by diverting that group.

Mental Health Australia chief executive Carolyn Nikoloski said supports were needed within the NDIS while also building a mental health system outside it for people with psychosocial conditions.

Without that, Ms Nikoloski said, "the strain simply shifts elsewhere".

"What we hope for is a clear and transparent plan for both how NDIS growth is to be managed within the stated targets, and how governments are finally going to deliver on their promise to deliver practical, meaningful support for the more than half a million people outside the NDIS with psychosocial disability who are currently missing out on vital mental health supports," she said.

"We have repeatedly been told that ministers take this matter seriously … yet to date we are still waiting for this solution and, with access to the NDIS potentially tightening even further, the need for substantial community-based mental health supports outside the NDIS is only going to increase."

Mr Butler would not comment on whether he would clarify supports for people with psychosocial disability in his Press Club address.

A meeting of health ministers in September is expected to progress a "foundational supports" scheme to be included as part of the next Mental Health Agreement, which is due by mid-next year.

State supports would cost $1bn extra

But establishing a new state-based service for psychosocial disability would also set the stage for a new round of fighting between governments, which continue to argue over the Thriving Kids program to redirect children with autism to state services, despite the rapidly approaching deadline for those services to be up and running.

The Productivity Commission warned last year that state and territory expenditure would have to grow by up to $1.09 billion a year to meet the existing gaps in support and, given their limited capacity to raise revenue, "it is likely Australian government funding will be needed to support this expenditure growth".

The commission said a funding split would have to be negotiated, though states and territories should hold sole responsibility for managing psychosocial supports outside the NDIS.

Professor Hickie said today was a "critical juncture" for the NDIS and called on the Commonwealth and states to work together.

But despite the commission's recommendation that supports be established as a matter of urgency for a group "in limbo", state governments have already pushed back on a fast-tracked process, saying that beginning those reforms before the conclusion of other health and disability negotiations, such as Thriving Kids, would risk undermining the overarching system.

On Tuesday New South Wales Premier Chris Minns warned the Commonwealth not to simply shift costs onto the states.

"We can't have a situation where people are knocked off the NDIS, and then the state provides the service because it's still coming out of the same pockets of NSW taxpayers, so we have to have a sustainable system," he said.

Chris Minns is urging the federal government not to let people fall through the cracks. (AAP Image: Bianca De Marchi)

Shadow NDIS Minister Melissa McIntosh questioned how people would be supported if they lost access to the NDIS.

"If the government's answer is to push people out of the NDIS, where are they supposed to go?" she asked.

"The reality is, whether it's the NDIS, Medicare or the broader health system, the supports people need simply are not there. You either qualify for the NDIS, or you fall into the state's black hole."

Ms Zanella said if people were again left in limbo by health and disability minister "buck passing", the cost would ultimately come back to them from hospital wards.

"The reality is this will hit health ministers, in every jurisdiction because the place of last resort where these people will end up going is in our emergency departments," she said.

"It will be EDs and tertiary hospitals that will have to [bear] the brunt. We will simply pass the problem from one area to another area with no good outcome in between."

World.title: ‘I have no regrets’: Your experiences with family estrangement
World.content:
Our recent story about the ambiguous loss that comes from family estrangement prompted many of you to share your own experiences.

Estrangement is the emotional or physical separation between people where a formerly close relationship becomes distant, hostile, or ceases entirely.

Whether you're a parent, sibling, child or grandchild, you've revealed the effect it's had on your life.

'I have no regrets about closing the door'

"Around nine months ago I made the decision to cut ties with my father. He didn't like my passion for women's and LGBTQIA+ rights and dismissed my feelings about many other issues. I was forced to come out to him as a lesbian after intense interrogation. He refused to accept this part of my identity. I told him I didn't want to see him or speak to him for the foreseeable future. Christmas and Easter, as well as my birthday, are hard because I know that he's going to call." — Darcy

"I cut contact with my parents for what turned out to be a 12-month period. It was devastating but also indescribably liberating. The expectation they had of obedience and respect led to toxic familial relationships and the impact has been lifelong. I have no regrets about closing the door on them for a period of time; sometimes we all get to the point where we need to make ourselves a priority over the expectations of others. People leave bad romantic relationships, the same understanding should apply to familial relationship situations." — Anna

The grief of being estranged from a loved one Estrangement usually begins after a significant traumatic experience with a loved one, experts say.

A 'whole family structure' impacted

"My sister's marriage broke down during COVID lockdowns. My parents and her other siblings all tried to support her and her children in the ways that we thought best. But my sister believed that some of the family sided with the ex-husband and she ultimately moved many kilometres away and she shut off from most of the family. Although the remaining siblings are typically on good terms with each other, the issue of our estranged sibling has at times driven a wedge between us." — Blaire

"I've been estranged from my father since July last year. My younger brother, who I've always had a close relationship with, we're no longer on speaking terms either. It's had a severe impact on my already poor health. The worst part is I don't think there'll be any reconciliation despite my best efforts, and I fear that my dad will pass away one day with no resolution." — Ally

Adoption can feel like a lifetime of estrangement

"Adopted people know deeply the feeling of estrangement because we live it each day. We are legally estranged from our biological families through the processes of adoption. Often when we go searching for our family, we are refused contact and expected to follow strict contact rules, which perpetuate the shame and secrecy of our existence. Fathers don't know we exist and are alienated from us." — Jennifer

Finding support can be difficult

"I can say this has been the hardest of all things to deal with. There is little information on the internet, I couldn't find a support group and stories are often told from the perspective of the child, not the parent. You can't help blaming yourself and forever wondering, '"what did I do?'". I'm sure that there are thousands of parents out there suffering who would get some comfort from knowing they're not alone." — Joanna

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

"In 2015, our son announced by email that "for the foreseeable future" he would be cutting off all contact. Eleven years later we're still totally in the dark and rely on third parties to assure us he's even alive. It's been horrible." — Leon

Terminal illness led me to reconnect with my mother

Going low or no contact with family Family dynamics can be complicated and going 'no contact' to avoid further conflict is often suggested on social media.

"Some would say my relationship with my mother was always estranged. Recently, Mum passed after a short battle with leukaemia. Before she died, I travelled to see her for the first time in five years and she got to meet my son. We shared more memorable moments together in those final days than possibly the previous 40-odd years. Her loss continues to bring me incredible grief, remorse, disappointment, and a variety of other emotions. Mum and I were very similar in our stubbornness, which was absolutely to our detriment in this instance." — Stephan

'I've accepted my parents' flaws

"No contact was the healthiest decision I made with my parents. Perpetuating a toxic relationship is not healthy for either party. There was always an incredibly unhealthy dynamic where any mention of my childhood would set my parents off. I've been able to accept that my parents are just people, and that despite their flaws they were just trying their best. Cutting contact was like lifting a massive weight off my chest. It gave me the space to discover who my authentic self is." — Ben

World.title: When the tree-change dream becomes a nightmare, that’s Alphabet Lane
World.content:
CultureMoviesCinema When the tree-change dream becomes a nightmare, that’s Alphabet Lane Karl Quinn April 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

You can take the filmmaker out of the bush, but you can’t take the bush out of the filmmaker – just ask James Litchfield, whose debut feature Alphabet Lane absolutely reeks of his upbringing. Litchfield comes from a long line of pastoralists in the Monaro region in south-east New South Wales. His great-great-great-grandfather James Litchfield arrived from England in the 1860s and started raising sheep on a small block near Cooma; that small block has now grown to a multi-site empire across four states. The property has been passed from James to James to James over the generations, until this James decided his calling was in filmmaking (via the law), and sister Bea stepped into the gumboots instead. Will Johnston, left, as an old friend who visits Jack (Nicholas Denton, right) and Anna in the country. His family was “extremely supportive” of his decision to trade the shears for the lens, says James, whose film was shot on the family’s Hazeldean Litchfield Estate. “I knew I wanted to make something on the Monaro,” he says. “I grew up there, I’ve got a certain connection to the place, and a lot of emotions to tap into.”



His film, privately financed and made for less than $1 million, is a funny, spare and emotionally complex tale of a young professional couple who make the tree change from Sydney to the Monaro region and find it a lot more challenging than they’d ever imagined. It nudges at thriller and horror territory but ultimately is a surprisingly inventive relationship drama. Anna (Tilda Cobham-Hervey) is a doctor doing the night shift at the local hospital. Jack (Nicholas Denton) is an engineer on the Snowy Hydro Scheme, driving miles from the fabulous bluestone homestead they’re renting to the site each day. We first meet them on a dusty road as they’re heading to and from work, stopping for an early morning hello full of longing and love. Later in the film, as they pass without even acknowledging each other, we know the relationship is in big trouble. The crisis is triggered by the most innocuous of things: an imaginary friend conjured by Jack as a way of adding some spice to their lives, and filling the void of loneliness and isolation that’s crept in, though neither wants to admit it. It would be fair, then, to say the film evinces a certain ambivalence to the place, right?



“The landscape for me is so fascinating because it’s very beautiful, but it’s also really cold, it’s windy, it’s sort of dry,” says Litchfield. “It makes such an amazing backdrop for this story of two people who are struggling to connect with where they are, and also have these little problems in their own relationship.” He wrote the screenplay in his mid-30s, at a time when lots of his friends “had moved overseas or moved city or moved to the country or changed careers, or were at that point where they’re finding a new life. And a lot of them were finding there’s a lot of difficulties that come with that”. He says the device of the imaginary friend – who turns out to have a wife, who also enters the increasingly strange dynamic between Jack and Anna – echoes something he has observed in real-world relationships. “A lot of couples seem to have a third thing,” he says. “It’s often some sort of shared creative project. Couples who don’t have kids might have a dog that becomes quite an important character in their relationship, and they sometimes ventriloquise the dog and use it to negotiate certain things.” That was, he says “the vague, rough concept” he set out to explore.



Lucinda Reynolds was working at Amazon when the script landed on her desk. Having grown up in the country herself, she saw things in it that both struck a chord and took her by surprise. “I thought, ‘Oh, my God, this is so unique and alive’,” she says “It was very psychological. I felt it existed in this canon of Australian films about not belonging in a place, but it felt very contemporary and fresh too. James Litchfield directs Tilda Cobham-Hervey on the set of Alphabet Lane. “I have lots of friends who have done this tree change,” she adds. “And I love anything that speaks to that conversation between urban and rural lives in Australia.” She also liked that it would be a fun project for a small cast, was largely contained to a handful of locations, and would be possible to make with a small crew and budget – perfect, in other words, for her first outing as producer.



What she didn’t anticipate was that she and Litchfield would end up becoming a couple. “I wouldn’t not advise it, but I wouldn’t tell everyone to do it,” she says of falling in love and making a movie at the same time. “Making a film is like making a family, it’s so intense. For us, it worked; I think we do work quite nicely together. And when you find the people you work well with, it’s a bit of a gift.” Alphabet Lane is in cinemas from April 23 Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Victoria’s new child safety regulator runs into FIFO controversy
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaChild safety Victoria’s new child safety regulator runs into FIFO controversy Kieran Rooney and Grant McArthur April 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The state government has been criticised for appointing a fly-in, fly-out bureaucrat to oversee the first steps in overhauling Victoria’s problem-plagued childcare sector. Brisbane-based Adam Fennessy became the interim regulator of the Victorian Early Childhood Regulatory Authority (VECRA) in January, a new version of the watchdog created after damning failures in the sector were exposed by charges against accused paedophile Joshua Brown. Adam Fennessy has been commuting between Brisbane and Melbourne since he was appointed as Victoria’s interim childcare regulator. Marija Ercegovac It was part of a range of regulatory reforms made by the government to deliver an unprecedented level of oversight and enforcement over childcare providers. While the job is based in Melbourne, Fennessy has travelled back to Brisbane almost every weekend and been spotted in the Queensland capital on Fridays and even mid-week.



He has not hidden his trips home from the public, instead regularly posting his exercise routines on Strava, a social media app for runners which details their location and routes. But some within the sector and the state opposition have questioned why the government would select someone – even on a short-term basis – who was not based in Victoria for a public interest role meant to create the perception of a strong commitment to safety reform. Joshua Brown has been charged with sex offences in Victoria over his time working as a childcare worker. Marija Ercegovac The government also came under fire last year when this masthead revealed the boss of Victoria’s Suburban Rail Loop project commuted from Queensland, and billed taxpayers for some of his costs to travel to Melbourne. He left the job a month later. Two senior sources, who have both worked with Fennessy in multiple roles over the past decade, expressed concern that he had been appointed to a role demanding the highest commitment and attention.



The sources, who were not approved to speak publicly, agreed Fennessy was well liked across state and federal bureaucracies as well as the political spectrum, but he had no experience in the early childhood sector and a recent history splitting his time between states. “How the regulator’s office is set up matters. You would have thought they need someone with both experience and a presence in Victoria,” one said. “It is critical that somebody with an understanding of the sector is establishing it the right way in order for it to go forward. “Adam is an experienced bureaucrat, but he has never worked in childcare, he has never worked in social policy or early childhood, he has always worked in environment.” Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said: “Ensuring the safety of children and restoring community confidence in Victoria’s childcare sector is not FIFO job.



A post on Adam Fennessy’s Strava account. “Following the heartbreaking allegations of horrific misconduct within childcare settings last year and the failings of the government’s regulator, Victorians rightfully expect this role be located in Victoria on a full-time basis.” A source working in Victoria’s childhood sector, who was not approved to speak publicly, said Fennessy had been a visible presence in Melbourne meetings since taking on the regulatory position. The source added that he had been open that his return to Melbourne was temporary and, as he was unable to relocate to Victoria permanently, he would not apply for the ongoing position. After this masthead sent questions to the Allan government about Fennessy’s travel arrangements, he changed his Strava settings to private. Fennessy has been training for the Brisbane Half Marathon, with records showing him in Brisbane regularly in January, including the Tuesday and Wednesday following the Australia Day public holiday.



His Strava profile indicates he is regularly in Brisbane early enough on Fridays to take afternoon walks. The night before Good Friday, he was at the Gabba for Brisbane’s victory over Collingwood, posting on Strava: “Kick to kick after the footy then walking home.” Responding to questions from this masthead, a spokesperson for the Department of Education said Fennessy was based in Melbourne. “Adam Fennessy relocated to Melbourne when he took up the role of Interim Regulator at VECRA on 1 January 2026,” they said. Loading “Neither the Department of Education or VECRA have paid for reunion flights or personal travel expenses for Mr Fennessy.



“It is anticipated the Governor-In-Council will soon be appointing a permanent regulator, who will continue to be Victorian-based.” The department did not comment further when presented with Fennessy’s Strava profile. Fennessy did not respond when contacted directly by this masthead. A source close to the recruitment process, speaking anonymously to detail internal deliberations, said interstate applicants had been discouraged from applying for the position as the permanent regulator, who should be appointed by the end of the financial year. Adam Fennessy was appointed to the Victorian Early Childhood Regulatory Authority on an interim basis. DELWP A state government source said it was generally considered appropriate to make exceptional provisions for people who had a high standard of expertise in a field, but that this was a difficult test to apply to Fennessy.



The Department of Education would not reveal Fennessy’s remuneration for the interim position, which he took on after finishing up as the secretary of the federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF) in September. Related Article Exclusive

Education Loopholes in national child safety reforms raise red flags about sex abuse risks At a Senate estimates hearing last October, acting DAFF secretary Justine Saunders was asked whether Fennessy’s commuting from Brisbane was a factor in his departure from the role. She said she was not aware of any concerns. Under further questions, acting deputy secretary Tim Simpson revealed it was a condition of Fennessy’s employment that he was based in Canberra, and said he was confident it had been met. “As part of his condition with living in Canberra, he had reunion travel under the Remuneration Tribunal conditions to Brisbane, which was his home port, but he was based out of Canberra for the role,” Simpson said.



“I wouldn’t have specifics on that (how often he worked from the Canberra office), obviously, here at hand, but from my perspective he was in Canberra the vast majority of the time.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Hot or not: The best and worst recruits of the 2026 AFL season so far
World.content:
Money Talks SportAFLAFL 2026 Hot or not: The best and worst recruits of the 2026 AFL season so far Peter Ryan April 22, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Photo: Artists Bailey Smith helped Geelong to a grand final last season after being traded from the Western Bulldogs. Ben Brown and Bobby Hill helped Melbourne and Collingwood to flags in 2021 and 2023 in their first seasons with their new clubs. That’s why what happens in October matters, and why we spend the year analysing who might lure Zak Butters, Ben King or Zac Bailey to their club in 2027. It’s only the eve of round seven, but there is enough evidence to make some early judgments on who the hottest recruits are so far this season, and which players are battling to make the desired impact at this stage.



The good news for those who are struggling: They have plenty of time to find form. Last year’s trade period recruits who are running hot Christian Petracca after he booted a big goal against Essendon. AFL Photos Gold Coast’s Christian Petracca has played four of the Suns’ six games so far this season. They have won the four he has played, and lost the two he missed. He sits fourth in the coaches’ association award and has kicked a lazy 10 goals. He also averages 11.5 score involvements, the leading player on that front. Melbourne’s Jack Steele looked like Richmond great Geoff Raines when he stormed out of a centre clearance and kicked long twice in the first quarter against the Brisbane Lions. Steele cost nothing at the draft table and is taking up little in terms of total player payments (TPP). A good person around the club is proving the right fit at the right time. The Giants’ Clayton Oliver had to step up after Tom Green’s knee injury, and he has been impressive in a battling team. After an excellent opening against Hawthorn, he has worked hard to stem the tide in games the Giants have lost. Honorable mentions go to Port Adelaide’s Corey Durdin and Melbourne’s Brody Mihocek, with 10 goals apiece, Sydney’s Jai Serong, who has proved a handful on the wing, and St Kilda’s Sam Flanders, who is playing to expectation at the moment. Finnbar Maley is proving a surprise, albeit ungainly, performer at the Crows.



Tom De Koning has had his moments in his new colours but is yet to fire. AFL Photos The recruits running cold The obvious one is St Kilda’s Tom De Koning, who has looked out of sorts in the past two matches, with injury potentially the reason he is dropping marks and not reaching hitouts. He hasn’t earned a coaches’ vote and has kicked one goal. He is capable of more but is yet to find form. The Brisbane Lions’ Oscar Allen played an excellent game against Collingwood after a slow start to his career at his new club. But he is taking time to find his feet as the Lions’ key forward. On the upside, he has not missed a match and has shown enough of his ability in glimpses to give reason for some optimism. Collingwood’s Jack Buller did not cost much at the trade table, but he has not yet proved a replacement for Mihocek, as many had hoped. He was out of the side after round one and is not smashing the door down to get back into a misfiring forward line. West Coast’s Brandon Starcevich has been injured and is not due back until mid-season. Sydney’s Charlie Curnow is up and down but has been threatening and is helping his teammates. He remains a watch, however, given how much draft capital the Swans expended on him.



Playing as expected Carlton traded in six players but none have been able to turn around the Blues’ fortunes, although none are playing below what they showed at their previous clubs. The Saints’ Jack Silvagni and Liam Ryan have been par. Jamarra Ugle-Hagan was always going to take time and is yet to break into the Suns’ team. A free agent running hot at the right time Melbourne free agent Kade Chandler has put any contract discussions to the back of his mind as he flourishes as a high half-forward under Steven King after three consecutive seasons of solid football. The 26-year-old earned eight coaches’ votes for his match-winning performance against the Brisbane Lions. He kicked two big goals in a tight final quarter to add to his one in the second term, which was Melbourne’s only major for that quarter.



Melbourne’s Kade Chandler is a free agent in form. Getty Images The consistent performer has played 23 matches a year in each of the past three seasons and looks likely to remain a Demon, however he is sure to attract interest from other clubs if his good form continues this year. “I feel really confident in my game, and I feel like my teammates trust me each and every week to just get my role done,” Chandler said. But he is leaving the contract discussions to when he feels the time is right.



“I have not thought about it too much. I am absolutely loving my footy, and I am just focused on getting a few more wins under the belt,” Chandler told Money Talks. “I am sure those conversations will start when the time comes, but at the moment I am happy having a win with the boys, and I am looking forward to the rest of the year.” His teammate and fellow South Australian Tom Sparrow is also a free agent being monitored by South Australian clubs. A mature-age Bomber Essendon’s Tom Edwards has made a great start to his post-ACL injury career with the Bombers. He has kicked two goals in each of his three matches since his return against the Western Bulldogs coincided with the team’s return to competitiveness. Tom Edwards has been impressive in his return from a knee reconstruction. AFL Photos



The Bombers showed their faith in the West Australian after just two games when they extended his contract to the end of this season soon after his knee injury, but they are yet to open discussions with the now 25-year-old who has leadership potential and could command more later in the season if he keeps performing at the same pace throughout.
